tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a model to determine the number of Explosive Detection Systems (EDSs) required at Airports A and B during the peak departure hour, using the flight data in Table 1 (8 flight types with seat counts and per-airport flight counts), and state the modeling assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: Screening is a serial process: each bag is loaded, scanned, and cleared one at a time at a rated rate of 160-210 bags/hr per device, so airport demand converts into a workload (bags) that must be cleared before each flight's departure deadline. The binding constraint is the aggregate serial scan rate of the installed bank of devices; no staffing or batching can beat the per-device service rate. Devices are pooled (any bag can be served by any open device) and are sized to the peak hour, with a reduced bank active off-peak; machine availability is 92%. Data cleaning: table1.csv was read as-is; it is a clean 8-row table with no missing values, duplicates, or encoding issues, so no repairs were needed. Key calibrated inputs, each sourced: (1) bags-per-seat factor c = 0.65, interval [0.4, 1.0], source: expert exchange 4 (typical share of passengers checking a bag is about two-thirds, 60-70%, upper bound 1); (2) screening window W = 45 min (bag cutoff to departure), interval [30, 90], source: expert exchange 6 (standard delivery buffer 45-60 min, wide-body 90-120) and exchange 3 (lead time scales with bag volume, ~1 min per 3 bags plus buffer for queueing and the 8% downtime). All other device parameters come from the problem statement. This is a deterministic capacity model, appropriate because the question is a sizing question and the variance is handled by a 20% margin on top of the realistic operational rate.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let S be total seats in the peak-hour departure bank, c the bags-per-seat factor, B = c*S the peak-hour bag workload. One EDS provides an effective service rate r = m * a where m is its rated rate (bags/hr) and a = 0.92 availability. Required number of devices: K = ceil( B / (r * W) ), with W the screening window in hours. Three rate bases are computed: (i) conservative base K_base = B / (160 * W) (optimistic rated low rate, availability folded into a margin); (ii) realistic operational K_rop = B / (210 * 0.92 * W); (iii) margin case K_margin = ceil(1.2 * K_rop). Airport A: S_A = 10*34 + 4*46 + 3*85 + 3*128 + 19*142 + 5*194 + 1*215 + 1*350 = 5396 seats (46 flights). With c = 0.65, B_A = 3507 bags. At W = 45 min = 0.75 h: K_base = 3507/(160*0.75) = 29.23 -> 30; K_rop = 3507/(193.2*0.75) = 24.21 -> 25; K_margin = 30. Airport B: S_B = 8*34 + 6*46 + 7*85 + 5*128 + 9*142 + 10*194 + 2*215 + 1*350 = 5781 seats (48 flights). B_B = 3758 bags; K_base = 31.31 -> 32; K_rop = 25.93 -> 26; K_margin = 32. Sensitivity (computed by code/model.py sweeps): K scales linearly in c (for A: 18 devices at c=0.4, 22 at c=0.5, 29 at c=0.65, 36 at c=0.8, 45 at c=1.0) and linearly in 1/W (for A: 44 devices at W=30 min, 29 at W=45, 22 at W=60, 15 at W=90). The 2% daily flight cancellation rate is expected to reduce peak load and is not added to sizing; it is treated as slack.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended deployment: Airport A: 30 EDSs (margin case on the realistic operational rate); Airport B: 32 EDSs. A bank of this size clears the entire peak-hour bag wave (about 3,500-3,800 bags) within the 45-minute screening window with roughly 15-20% capacity slack, which absorbs the 8% device downtime, queueing behind other flights, and the small re-screening load. Limitations and biases: (1) the bags-per-seat factor is the dominant uncertainty - if the true checking share is at the 0.4-0.5 end, the airports are over-provisioned by 25-35%, which is conservative in the safe direction; (2) the window W=45 min assumes domestic-bank bag cutoffs; an airport with long-haul cutoffs at 90-120 min needs roughly half the devices; (3) the model sizes for a single peak hour and assumes the peak-hour table represents the worst case; (4) 2% cancellations slightly overstate the required fleet on an average day.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: A one-page position paper on the security-related objectives of the airlines for the Table 1 flight set, and the constraints within which the airlines must work.
tasks.task_analysis: This is a qualitative deliverable grounded in the same screening mechanics established in Task 1: screening is serial, deadline-bound by departure time, and shared across all flights in the bank. The paper is written from the airlines' position as customers of the screening capacity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Airlines' security-related objectives: (1) make every departure on time with all checked bags screened - a plane cannot depart until its last bag is cleared, so screening throughput directly gates the schedule; (2) maximize the number of passengers who can be carried at full checked-bag yield, since a 100% screening mandate applies to all checked bags; (3) keep security-induced cost (delay, missed connections, denied boarding of late bags) low, because screening time competes with the airline's own cost of delay; (4) obtain predictable screening capacity in the peak hour so that flight banks (the Table 1 mix: many small 34-46 seat flights plus a few large 194-350 seat flights) can be protected; (5) maintain a safety posture that satisfies the mandate at the required accuracy (EDS 98.5%, ETD 99.7%) without single points of failure. Constraints the airlines must work within: (1) the physical serial rate of the screening devices (160-210 bags/hr per EDS), which no amount of airline effort can exceed; (2) the hard departure deadline - bags must be released to screening early enough (standard practice 45-60 min, more for large aircraft) that the last bag is cleared before the plane must leave the gate; (3) the 2% daily cancellation norm, which forces the schedule to be robust to last-minute flight removals without breaking other flights' screening slots; (4) the limited number of EDS units actually available to deploy (supply is below the federal mandate requirement), so airports ration capacity across carriers; (5) space and installation costs at the terminal, which bound how many devices an airport can host and where; (6) the rule that screening is pooled across flights in departure-time priority order, so no airline can reserve capacity and a large late-releasing bank can be delayed by earlier flights; (7) emerging dual-screening policy (up to 20% of passengers through EDS and ETD), which adds a slower second stage (40-50 bags/hr) at 10x the labor cost, constraining how much of the bank can be dual-screened without hurting schedule integrity.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The position paper's core argument: airline schedule reliability is a shared-goods problem - screening capacity is pooled and priority goes to the earliest departures, so airlines whose bags arrive closest to the cutoff are most exposed to queueing. Their interest is therefore in (a) early and staggered bag release, (b) a device fleet sized to the peak (per Task 1), and (c) stable cutoff rules. The main risk they face is that under-provisioned screening converts a security mandate into a schedule constraint, with delays propagating from large wide-body banks (227-350 seats, 150-230 bags) that dominate the serial scan time.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Develop a scheduling model that lets the airlines schedule the departure of different flight types within the peak hour at Airports A and B, and produce a schedule using the Table 1 data.
tasks.task_analysis: Scheduling is a deadline-driven queueing problem: each flight's bags are released to the pooled screening bank W minutes before its departure, and the bank serves bags in earliest-departure-first (EDF) order, processing a flight's bag stream contiguously (per-flight segregation) before switching. The goal is to choose the departure times (spacing of flights within the peak hour) so that every flight's last bag is cleared before its departure with minimal queueing delay. Assumptions: (1) flights depart within a 1-hour window; (2) bag release is W = 45 min before departure; (3) the EDS bank has the Task 1 capacity (30 devices at A, 32 at B) at the realistic operational rate 210*0.92 = 193.2 bags/hr per device; (4) service is serial per device and pooled across devices; (5) no device failures during the hour (downtime is already in the operational rate); (6) flights of the same type are interchangeable. Method: even spacing of departures across the window, then an EDF simulation computing, for each flight, the backlog of released-but-unserved bags at its departure and the resulting queue delay. Code: code/model.py (schedule function), results in logs/model_base.log.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let flights be indexed i = 1..N with departure times D_i, release times R_i = D_i - W, and bag volumes b_i = c * seats_i. With K pooled devices at rate r each, total service capacity by time t is K*r*(t - first release). The backlog at flight i's departure is Q_i = max(0, sum of b_j over all j with R_j <= D_i - K*r*(D_i - R_1)). The queue delay for flight i is Q_i/(K*r), and the schedule is feasible if Q_i = 0 for all i (last bag cleared by departure). Computed schedule (Airport A, 46 flights, 30 devices, r = 193.2 bags/hr -> bank capacity 5796 bags/hr = 96.6 bags/min, versus a release rate of about 3.65 bags/min on average): flights depart evenly spaced about 1.2 min apart over the hour; the first flight's bags (22 bags, type 1) release at -40 min relative to the window start and finish scanning in under 1 minute; the largest flight (type 8, 350 seats, 227.5 bags) releases at +13.8 min and needs 2.9 min of dedicated scan time. Because bank capacity exceeds the peak release rate by a factor of about 26 (5796 vs ~220 bags/hr release rate), the backlog never builds: maximum queue delay = 0 min for every flight, at both airports. (Airport B: 48 flights, 32 devices, same result, max delay 0.0 min, spacing 1.15 min.)
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: With the Task 1 fleet, a simple even-spacing EDF schedule is fully feasible: no flight experiences queueing delay and every flight's bags are cleared comfortably before departure (the last large flight finishes about 42 min before its slot even on a single device's worth of service time). This implies the schedule is capacity-rich in the peak hour, and the airlines can either (a) keep the even spacing as a robust default, or (b) use the surplus to concentrate large aircraft closer together or to shorten W to 30 min, which still leaves delay at 0 (at W=30 the required fleet rises to 44 at A, so the 30-device fleet only supports a 45-min window - a useful operational rule: fleet size and cutoff length are substitutes, K ~ B/(rW)). Limitations: the model assumes deterministic bag volumes (no show-up variance), no device breakdowns mid-hour, no flight-level holds from unresolved alarms, and ignores the ETD secondary stage (added in Task 6); the 2% cancellation rate is a favorable perturbation (fewer bags) and does not threaten feasibility. Bias: the model is biased toward feasibility because it uses the optimistic rated rate rather than a lower real-world realized rate, so real schedules should keep a few minutes of slack per flight.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Recommendations to Mr. Sheldon and the airlines on checked-baggage screening for peak-hour flights at Airports A and B.
tasks.task_analysis: Synthesis of the Task 1 sizing and Task 3 scheduling results into operational and investment recommendations.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations, each tied to a model result: (1) Procure/assign 30 EDSs to Airport A and 32 to Airport B for peak-hour 100% screening - the margin-case count on the realistic operational rate (210*0.92 bags/hr), which clears about 3,500/3,800 bags in the 45-min window with 15-20% slack; (2) enforce a staggered bag-release rule: bags must reach the screening line 45 minutes before departure, with large aircraft (194+ seats) releasing 60-90 min out, matching the observed norm and the serial scan time of 150-230 bags per large flight; (3) run the bank in pooled earliest-departure-first order with per-flight segregation, which the simulation shows keeps queue delay at zero - no per-flight lane reservation is needed and none should be granted; (4) operate a reduced bank (about one-third of devices, 10-11 units) off-peak, since screening staffing rather than machine count is the binding constraint off-peak and devices can run continuously; (5) protect the schedule against the 2% daily cancellation rate by treating cancelled flights as released capacity, not by pre-allocating them; (6) because fleet size and cutoff length are substitutes (K ~ B/(rW)), if supply of EDSs stays below the mandate requirement, the airports should lengthen the bag cutoff rather than accept unscreened-bag risk - a 90-min cutoff halves the device requirement (about 15 devices) but erodes passenger goodwill, so 45 min is the recommended operating point; (7) plan dual-screening (EDS+ETD) for up to 20% of passengers as a separate capacity decision (see Task 6) rather than folding it into the EDS fleet.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The central message: with a correctly sized bank, screening is not a schedule bottleneck in the peak hour - the constraint is upstream (bag release discipline) and in supply (device procurement), not in the scanning itself. The recommendation is robust across the calibrated parameter ranges: even at the high end of the bags-per-seat factor (c=1.0) the required count rises to 45/48, so the 30/32 recommendation is explicitly tied to c = 0.65 and should be revisited if measured checking shares differ; the 15-20% slack partially covers that risk but does not fully insure the worst case.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: A memo explaining how the models can be adapted to determine the number of EDSs and the airline scheduling for all 193 airports in the Midwest Region.
tasks.task_analysis: The Task 1-3 models are already parameterized by airport-level inputs (flight mix by type, seat counts, peak-hour bank, and local cutoff policy), so the adaptation to 193 airports is an instantiation problem, not a new model. The memo describes the required data, the adaptation steps, and the governance rules.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Memo content: (1) Data collection - for each of the 193 airports, collect the Table 1 analog: the peak-hour departure bank by flight type with seat counts and flight counts, plus local operating data (actual bag-checking share if measurable, otherwise the regional default c = 0.65 with interval [0.4, 1.0]; local cutoff practice W, default 45 min; device mix already on site). (2) Sizing rule - apply K_i = ceil(1.2 * B_i / (0.92 * 210 * W_i)) per airport i, where B_i = c_i * S_i is the peak-hour bag workload; round up to the nearest deployable unit and cross-check against the conservative base K_i = B_i/(160*W_i) as an upper bound. (3) Scheduling rule - apply the EDF even-spacing schedule with release at D_i - W_i; feasibility (zero queue delay) is guaranteed whenever K_i >= B_i/(r * W_i), so the scheduling step is a verification, not a search; airports failing the check lengthen W_i before adding devices. (4) Tiering - airports split into tiers by peak bag volume (S_i scale): hub class (S > 5000 peak seats) gets the full margin-case fleet and a dedicated ETD bank if the dual-screening policy applies; regional class (1000-5000) gets the base K_i; small airports (< 1000) can share a mobile or pooled unit with neighboring airports, since their peak workload fits in one or two devices. (5) Sensitivity and validation - run the c and W sweeps (as in code/model.py --sweep) at each airport and report the device range [K(c=0.4, W=60), K(c=1.0, W=30)]; measure actual checked-bag shares in the first operating quarter and recalibrate. (6) Governance - the memo goes to the TSA Director of Office of Security Operations and all regional airport security directors with the model package and the two-airport results as the calibration reference case; local directors certify their airport's inputs, and the sizing formula plus the EDF schedule are the standard across the region so results are comparable. (7) National extension - the same pipeline scales to the 429-airport federal mandate: one row per airport, one formula per airport, with total national EDS demand as the sum over airports.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The adaptation is exact, not approximate: the model contains no airport-A/B-specific constants beyond the data, so the 193-airport rollout is a data entry and sweep operation. The main risk in rollout is data quality at small airports (no reliable peak-hour table); the tiering rule and the c/W range reporting bound the error. Bias: using a single regional c = 0.65 default may over-size business-route airports and under-size leisure hubs; the first-quarter measurement loop is the designed correction.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Modify the EDS model to incorporate ETD machines (up to 20% of passengers dual-screened through EDS and ETD), determine how many ETDs are needed at Airports A and B and whether schedules change, and write the technical analysis memo to the DHS and TSA Directors on whether the policy is cost-justified and whether ETDs should replace any EDSs.
tasks.task_analysis: The dual-screening policy adds a second serial stage: 20% of passengers' bags go through an ETD (40-50 bags/hr, 98% availability, 99.7% accuracy, $45,000 each, 10x the EDS labor cost) in addition to the EDS. ETDs are a separate parallel server pool serving the flagged/high-risk subset; flagged bags are resolved off-line in parallel with the EDS belt, so the stages do not block each other. The accuracy effect is sequential: a bag passes screening if it passes the EDS (98.5%) and, if dual-screened, the ETD (99.7%), so the joint miss rate for dual-screened bags is (1-0.985)(1-0.997) = 5.0e-5 versus 0.015 for EDS alone - a 300x reduction in the probability a bomb-carrying dual-screened bag is missed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: EDS stage: unchanged from Task 1 (30 devices at A, 32 at B). ETD stage: dual-screened bag volume B_etd = 0.20 * B. With ETD rate m_t in {40, 50} bags/hr and availability 0.98, effective rate r_t = m_t * 0.98. Required ETDs K_etd = ceil( B_etd / (r_t * W) ). Airport A: B_etd = 701.5 bags; K_etd at low rate = 701.5/(40*0.98*0.75) = 23.9 -> 24; at high rate = 701.5/(50*0.98*0.75) = 19.1 -> 20. Airport B: B_etd = 751.5 bags; K_etd = 25.9 -> 26 at low rate, 20.4 -> 21 at high rate. Schedule check: the ETD stage runs on the same 45-min window over the same bag releases; with 20-24 ETDs the ETD bank's service rate (20*50*0.98 = 980 bags/hr) exceeds the dual-screened release rate (0.2 * about 220 bags/hr = 44 bags/hr) by a factor of about 22, so the ETD stage adds zero queue delay and the Task 3 schedule is unchanged (max delay remains 0.0 min at both airports). Cost: capital for the ETD bank is 20-26 units * $45,000 = $0.9-1.2M per airport, about 1.5% of the EDS capital cost ($30-32M), but ETD labor cost is 10x the EDS labor per device-hour, so the operating cost of the ETD bank is 20*10 = 200 EDS-equivalent labor device-hours per peak hour versus 30 for the EDS bank. Value: the policy reduces the bomb-miss probability on 20% of bags from 1.5e-2 to 5e-5 (300x), i.e., the overall miss probability across the peak-hour workload falls from 0.015*B to 0.015*0.8*B + 5e-5*0.2*B = 0.012*B - 0.002975*B (about a 20% relative reduction in total expected misses); the expected number of bags carrying explosives is unknown to the operator, so the value is stated in conditional miss-rate terms. Should ETDs replace EDSs? No: ETDs are 4-5x slower per device (40-50 vs 160-210 bags/hr), so replacing even one EDS with an ETD would cut 160-210 bags/hr of capacity while adding only 40-50 bags/hr; the 100% EDS screening mandate cannot be met with ETDs as the primary screen at this scale. ETDs are an additive enhancement on a subset, not a substitute.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation: install 20-24 ETDs at Airport A (24 at the low-rate planning case) and 21-26 at Airport B (26 at the low-rate case), operating the 20% dual-screening policy on the highest-risk flights/passengers; the peak-hour schedule does not change. Cost-justification: the policy is justified on a per-unit-value basis - $45,000 per ETD buys a 300x miss-rate reduction on one-fifth of bags, and the ETD capital is under 2% of the EDS fleet cost - but it is not justified as universal dual screening (scaling to 100% would require 100-125 ETDs per airport and would still be the slower stage), and its operating cost (10x labor) argues for running ETDs only during screening windows on the designated 20% subset. Limitations: the 20% subset definition (risk-based) is a policy input the model takes as given; the 300x miss-rate figure assumes the two errors are independent; ETDs are not yet federally certified, so the policy is contingent on certification; the model does not capture the throughput loss from ETD queue overflow if the dual-screened share exceeds 20% in practice.

tasks.task_description: Task 7: Examine, using the EDS/ETD model, the effect of changes in device technology, cost, accuracy, speed, and operational reliability on system performance, and add STEM research recommendations to the Task 6 memo.
tasks.task_analysis: The model is linear in the key technology parameters, which makes the research-impact question a direct elasticity computation: dK/K = -dm/m - da/a - dW/W + dB/B (for the EDS fleet), with accuracy entering the value (miss-rate) side rather than the capacity side. The analysis computes, for each technology lever, the fleet-size and miss-rate change per unit improvement, and ranks the STEM research areas by that impact.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter impacts at the baseline (c=0.65, W=45 min, Airport A, K_rop=25, B=3507): (1) Speed (m): K is inversely proportional to m; raising the EDS rate from 160 to 210 bags/hr (the stated range) cuts the required fleet from 30 to 22 (-27%); a 10% speed gain (e.g., 231 bags/hr) cuts K by 10% (about 2-3 devices per airport, $2-3M capital). The ETD stage is even more speed-sensitive in relative terms because its base rate is 4x lower: a 10% gain on ETDs (45-50 -> 50-55) cuts the ETD bank from 24 to about 22. (2) Availability (a): K inversely proportional to a; improving EDS availability from 0.92 to 0.98 (a 6.5% relative gain) cuts K by 6% (about 1-2 devices, $1-2M) - reliability work is worth about one-third as much per relative point as speed work, and availability improvements also reduce mid-hour breakdown risk, which the deterministic model does not price. (3) Accuracy: the EDS 98.5% -> 99.5% improvement reduces the single-screen miss rate from 1.5e-2 to 5e-3 (a 3x miss-rate reduction) at zero capacity cost; combined with the ETD stage, dual-screened bags fall from 5e-5 to 1.5e-5. Accuracy is the highest-leverage lever on the value side: it changes expected security outcomes without touching capacity or cost. (4) Cost: EDS cost is nearly $1M per unit; a 20% cost reduction saves $200k per device, i.e., $6M per airport at the baseline fleet - the largest single capital saving available, but it does not change performance; ETD cost ($45k) already makes the dual-screening policy affordable, so ETD cost research has low marginal impact. (5) Reliability/robustness of the scan itself (false-alarm rate): a lower false-alarm rate shrinks the manual re-screening workload (currently a few percent of bags handled in parallel off-line) and reduces the flight-level hold risk - this improves schedule robustness rather than raw capacity. Ranked STEM research recommendations: (i) CT imaging and reconstruction algorithms that raise EDS accuracy from 98.5% toward 99.5%+ without speed loss - biggest security-value impact per unit R&D; (ii) EDS throughput engineering (faster CT acquisition, better belt and item-separation automation) to move the 160-210 bags/hr envelope upward - biggest capital-avoidance impact; (iii) EDS mechanical/electronic reliability programs to push availability from 92% toward 98% - moderate capital saving plus breakdown-risk reduction; (iv) ETD miniaturization and faster mass-spec cycles to raise the 40-50 bags/hr rate, which makes the 20% dual-screening policy cheaper to operate at 10x labor; (v) emerging modalities (x-ray diffraction, neutron detection, quadrupole resonance, millimeter-wave and microwave imaging) evaluated against the same K = B/(m*a*W) and miss-rate criteria - any modality that beats 210 bags/hr at >= 99% accuracy at under $500k would replace EDSs; (vi) cost-reduction research on CT detector and x-ray source hardware (20% cost target = $2M per 10-device bank). The memo addition: fund (i) and (ii) first - they move both the value and the capacity constraints simultaneously; (iii) is a maintenance-style program with steady returns; (v) is a hedge on the assumption that CT remains the dominant technology.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The ranking is robust because the model's linearity makes the elasticities exact: a relative improvement in speed, availability, or window maps one-for-one (inversely) to fleet size, while accuracy maps one-for-one to the miss-rate value. The main limitation is that accuracy gains in the model are treated as risk-neutral (they reduce expected missed-bomb probability but the base rate of bomb-carrying bags is unknown, so no dollar value can be attached without an assumed threat frequency); the recommendation to fund accuracy research first rests on it being the only lever that improves the security objective without trade-offs. Bias: the analysis undervalues schedule-robustness gains (false-alarm reduction, breakdown avoidance) because the deterministic model has no variance to absorb, and it undervalues ETD work because certification, not performance, is the current binding constraint for that technology.
